w: At 4.2km, this is one of the longest commercial thoroughfares in Europe, and everything about Lodz grew up around it - the city took its present shape from this one straight axis. It fell into decay after the war, then was pedestrianised and revived after 1990 into the cafe strip locals call, half-jokingly, a cult.
s: One of Europe's longest shopping streets, reborn after 1990
_facts: Around 4.2km long, one of the longest commercial thoroughfares in Europe
Runs straight between Liberty Square and Independence Square
Was the axis around which the whole city grew; deteriorated after WWII
Revitalised into a pedestrian precinct after 1990

n: Archcathedral Basilica of St. Stanislaus Kostka
w: Lodz's archcathedral carries the name of a Polish Jesuit saint who died at nineteen, and it presides over the city's Catholic archdiocese from the same red-brick spires you can see from Piotrkowska Street. A minor basilica in a city better known for its factories than its churches.
s: The city's archcathedral, seat of the Lodz archdiocese
_facts: Archcathedral basilica located in Łódź, Łódź Voivodeship
Seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Łódź

w: Local textile barons paid for this Orthodox cathedral in the late 19th century as a gift to a small, easy-to-overlook Orthodox community in an overwhelmingly Catholic city. The payoff was an iconostasis shipped from St. Petersburg and an interior far more ornate than the modest congregation it served.
s: Industrialists' gift, with a St. Petersburg iconostasis
_facts: Polish Orthodox church built in the late 19th century
Built as a gift from local industrialists to Łódź's small Orthodox community
Richly decorated interior with an iconostasis manufactured in St. Petersburg

w: Opened in 1931 by Polish avant-garde artists, this was the first museum in Europe - and second in the world after MoMA - built specifically to collect modern art, spanning Cubism, Dada and Surrealism. Its Neoplastic Room, an experimental gallery for abstract art, opened in 1948 inside the old Poznanski family palace.
s: Europe's first dedicated modern art museum, since 1931
_facts: Founded 1931, opened as the International Collection of Modern Art by Polish avant-garde artists (a.r. group)
First museum in Europe, second in the world after MoMA, dedicated to modern art
Early collection spanned Cubism, Futurism, Dada, Surrealism, Formism and Unism
Moved to the Poznański family palace in 1948; Neoplastic Room opened the same year

w: Once the largest Jewish cemetery in Poland and among the biggest worldwide, this 44-hectare necropolis holds up to 230,000 marked graves plus mass graves from the Lodz ghetto and the Holocaust. The mausoleum of industrialist Izrael Poznanski - reputedly the largest Jewish tombstone anywhere - dominates the grounds.
s: Up to 230,000 graves, and the largest Jewish tombstone
_facts: Also known as the New Jewish Cemetery, opened 1892, covers around 44 hectares
Once the largest Jewish cemetery in Poland and among the largest worldwide
Contains 180,000-230,000 marked graves plus mass graves from the Litzmannstadt Ghetto and Holocaust
Mausoleum of industrialist Izrael Poznański is reputedly the largest Jewish tombstone in the world

w: A modest suburban railway station, built in the late 1920s for freight and passengers, became the loading platform from which the Lodz ghetto's Jews were sent to the extermination camps of Operation Reinhard. It stands today as a memorial, the tracks and platform left largely as they were.
s: The deportation platform for the Lodz ghetto
_facts: Also called Radogoszcz station, built 1926-1937
Served as the Umschlagplatz for deporting Jews from the Łódź Ghetto during Operation Reinhard
Located in Marysin, a neighbourhood in Łódź's Bałuty district; now a Holocaust memorial

w: German police and the Gestapo ran this prison through the whole of the occupation, and its name became shorthand for terror in wartime Lodz. Today it holds a museum commemorating the victims held and killed here between 1939 and 1945 - a grim counterpart, just across town, to the Radegast deportation platform.
s: A Gestapo prison, now a museum to its victims
_facts: German Order Police and Gestapo prison during the 1939-1945 occupation
German name Erweitertes Polizeigefängnis, Radegast
Now the site of a museum commemorating its wartime victims

w: Established in 1938 and still growing, this 16-hectare zoo is the only one in Poland to keep giant otters, Sumatran orangutans, false gharials and bush dogs alongside its more usual residents. Around 3,350 animals across 554 species make it one of the country's biggest wildlife collections.
s: Poland's only zoo with giant otters and false gharials
_facts: Established 1938, covers 16.64 hectares in the Polesie district
Home to around 3,350 animals representing 554 species
Only Polish zoo to feature giant otters, Sumatran orangutans, false gharials and bush dogs
Member of EAZA, WAZA and the International Species Information System

w: Lodz's largest theatre stages opera, operetta and ballet under one roof, a full repertory house built to match the industrial city's outsized ambitions in every other field. It remains the biggest stage in a city that once measured its wealth in cotton mills rather than curtain calls.
s: Lodz's biggest stage, for opera, operetta and ballet
_facts: Polish name Teatr Wielki w Łodzi (Grand Theatre)
Opera house; the largest theatre in the city
Specialises in opera, operetta and ballet

w: Built between 1835 and 1839 for textile magnate Ludwik Geyer, this classicist mill is considered the starting point of Lodz's industrial architecture - the building that set the template for the cotton empire that followed. It now houses the Central Museum of Textiles, telling the story it helped launch.
s: The building that kicked off Lodz's textile boom
_facts: Polish name Biała Fabryka, built 1835-1839 for Ludwik Geyer's textile factory complex
Considered an example of early industrial architecture in Łódź
Now hosts the Central Museum of Textiles and the Harnam Folk Dance Ensemble

w: Textile magnate Karol Scheibler's family built him a mausoleum grand enough to double as a landmark - a chapel raised in 1888 inside the Evangelical-Augsburg section of the Old Cemetery, designed by noted local architects. It stands as one of the clearest monuments to the industrial fortunes that built this city.
s: A textile baron's mausoleum, built like a landmark
_facts: Built 1888, designed by architects Edward Lilpop and Józef Pius Dziekoński
Located in the Evangelical-Augsburg part of the Old Cemetery, Ogrodowa Street
Chapel and mausoleum of industrialist Karl Wilhelm Scheibler

w: Poland's best-loved satirical poet sits forever on a bronze bench along Piotrkowska Street, life-size and approachable enough that passers-by sit down beside him for photos. Unveiled in 1998-1999, it turned a simple street sculpture into one of the most fondly touched monuments in the city.
s: A bronze bench with the poet Julian Tuwim, mid-sit
_facts: Also known as Tuwim's Bench (Lawka Tuwima), on Piotrkowska Street
Dedicated to poet Julian Tuwim
Constructed 1998-1999 by sculptor Wojciech Gryniewicz

w: This octagonal square marks the northern end of Piotrkowska Street and has done since 1823, decades before the street itself became Lodz's showcase. Its current name, Plac Wolnosci, dates to 1918 and Poland regaining independence - a rename that stuck through everything the 20th century threw at the city around it.
s: The octagonal square where Piotrkowska Street begins
_facts: Polish name Plac Wolności; octagonal public square in central Łódź
Completed 1823, the northern endpoint of Piotrkowska Street
Present name commemorates Poland regaining independence in 1918

w: Opened in 2004 on the 60th anniversary of the Lodz ghetto's liquidation, this park sits directly on former ghetto ground, honouring people who lived through it rather than those who did not. It is a rare kind of memorial: a living, green space built for survivors, not victims, in the valley where the ghetto stood.
s: A park for ghetto survivors, built on the ghetto's ground
_facts: Polish name Park Ocalałych, opened 30 August 2004, the 60th anniversary of the ghetto's liquidation
Commemorates people who survived the Łódź Ghetto
Located on former Łódź Ghetto territory, designed by Grażyna Ojrzyńska

w: Priest's Mill - the literal translation - is a whole district built for cotton, spinning mills and workers' housing raised from 1824 onward, once its own self-contained industrial world. Long neglected, it has spent the 21st century being converted into offices and flats, heritage repurposed rather than demolished.
s: A self-contained cotton-mill district, now being reborn
_facts: Name translates to Priest's Mill; area in the southern-central part of Łódź
Group of textile factories, mainly cotton spinning mills, built from 1824 onward
Undergoing major renovation and mixed-use redevelopment since the 2000s

w: A textile-boom mansion on Piotrkowska Street, built for and named after industrialist Juliusz Heinzl, has since traded cotton profits for civic bureaucracy: it is now the seat of Lodz's City Hall. Like much of the street around it, the palace's opulence was never about taste - it was about advertising money.
s: A textile baron's mansion, now Lodz's City Hall
_facts: Palatial mansion at 104 Piotrkowska Street
Named after its initial owner, industrialist Juliusz Heinzl
Now houses Łódź City Hall
